note: Cold-email building blocks: first-touch skeleton, framework picker, 6-touch sequence spine, subject-line formulas, anti-pattern list, seniority voice caps, domain-warming ramp, and metric triage rows. This bank is authored, not measured — the benchmark targets are widely-circulated rules of thumb, not results from our campaigns, and agents must not present anything here as 'proven'. A fuller step-by-step playbook with copy-paste prompts lives in the shared skills shelf as the cold-email-gtm skill; this bank is only the rows agents sample from. Hard rules that travel with every row: never fabricate a signal or proof point, drafts are queued for human approval before sending unless the operator explicitly authorized automated sends, and compliance rows are a checklist, not legal advice. Slots are UPPERCASE so an unfilled template trips the placeholder check in src/lib/services/deliverables/acceptance-contracts.ts.

volumeInfrastructure.rule: send from dedicated secondary domains, never the primary domain
volumeInfrastructure.detail: 10+ sending domains is a normal footprint for a scaled motion; the primary domain's reputation is never put at risk

volumeInfrastructure.rule: about 3 inboxes per domain, roughly 30 emails per day per inbox
volumeInfrastructure.detail: scale horizontally by adding domains and inboxes; never by pushing one mailbox harder
major-provider inboxes deliver; bargain SMTP does not

volumeInfrastructure.rule: never send cold email through newsletter or marketing ESPs
volumeInfrastructure.detail: opt-in marketing tools land cold mail in the promotions folder and lack sequence/reply mechanics; use a cold-email sequencer instead

deliverabilityPractices.why: open tracking injects an HTML pixel; plain-text mail delivers better, so reply rate becomes the primary metric at volume

deliverabilityPractices.practice: vary copy per recipient at volume (spintax)
deliverabilityPractices.why: byte-identical bodies sent to thousands get fingerprinted by filters; surface phrasing varies, meaning stays identical

deliverabilityPractices.practice: verify every address before sending, whatever the list source
deliverabilityPractices.why: bounces tell receiving servers you do not know who you are mailing

offerLevers.example: a named outcome with a number and a timeframe, never a category description of your services
an audit, mockup, trial, or consultation that makes the first yes easy without making the campaign a loss
if the audience does not need the offer, no rewrite saves the campaign; fix the offer or the segment first

escalationPlays.how: sequence non-responders get a LinkedIn connection touch where photo, profile, and mutuals raise trust; run under the linkedin bank's caps and human-approval rules
cold-email clicks land on a pixeled page; retarget visitors with case-study ads to stay present between touches at low cost
score each prospect's site against explicit fit criteria and personalise from scraped specifics before spending any sending volume on them

sequenceLengthFork: sources disagree: the craft motion runs 6 touches over 35 days; the volume motion caps at 2-3 touches and spends remaining capacity on new prospects. Choose per motion: high-personalisation low-volume gets the long sequence, high-volume broad gets the short one.

positioningSpectrum.soundsLike: we can build a system for you
positioningSpectrum.judgment: too much setup; the reader must believe in the process before feeling any outcome

positioningSpectrum.soundsLike: we run campaigns for companies like yours
positioningSpectrum.judgment: credible but centered on the sender, not the reader's result

positioningSpectrum.soundsLike: we're already talking to the kind of buyers you want more of
positioningSpectrum.judgment: target zone: active, in motion, close to the outcome the reader wants; use only when truthful

positioningSpectrum.soundsLike: I have clients ready for you tomorrow
positioningSpectrum.judgment: claim density collapses believability; pull back one step and anchor in what is genuinely in motion

positioningRule: move as close to the reader's desired outcome as credibility allows; the ceiling is what a realistic prospect would believe, never how bold the claim is, and a fabricated active position is off the table

languageLists.why: process language walks the reader backward through your work instead of forward to their result

languageLists.list: active-position phrasing to prefer when truthful
languageLists.why: in-motion language puts the reader next to the outcome; only usable when it is actually true

emailSkeleton.name: First-touch skeleton
emailSkeleton.template:
Subject: [TWO TO FOUR WORD SUBJECT THAT READS LIKE AN INTERNAL EMAIL]

[ONE SENTENCE ABOUT THEIR WORLD THAT NEVER STARTS WITH I OR WE]

[ONE OR TWO SENTENCES LINKING THEIR SITUATION TO YOUR OFFER]

[ONE SENTENCE OF SPECIFIC PROOF WITH A REAL NUMBER OR NAMED CUSTOMER]

[ONE LOW FRICTION QUESTION AS THE ONLY CTA]

[SIGN OFF]
emailSkeleton.why: Every line has exactly one job; a sentence that adds no curiosity, relevance, credibility, or ask gets cut.

frameworks.useWhen: The prospect has a visible pain point
frameworks.shape: problem observation, then relevance, then ask

frameworks.useWhen: A specific recent event: funding, hiring, news, job change
frameworks.shape: trigger reference, then connection to the problem, then ask

frameworks.useWhen: A referral or shared network exists
frameworks.shape: name drop, then context, then ask

frameworks.useWhen: You have something genuinely useful to share
frameworks.shape: insight or resource, then brief context, then ask
brief context, then one direct question; under 80 words

sequenceTouches.angle: new evidence: case study, data point, or recent result
a different but related pain point
industry insight tied to the problem
one direct question, no context or recap
breakup: professional close plus referral ask

sequenceRules: each touch brings a new angle
emails get shorter with each touch
never say checking in or circling back
subjectRules: no question marks by default; question-mark subjects are a known A/B variant, not a default
reads like an internal email between colleagues
never names your product or company
photograph principle: form one clear mental picture; clarity beats curiosity, curiosity beats clever

antiPatterns.pattern: Opening with your own name and company
antiPatterns.why: The reader does not care yet; the opener belongs to their world.
Passive filler that wastes the first line.
Announces that you searched a list.

antiPatterns.pattern: I hope this finds you well

antiPatterns.why: Could apply to anyone, so it lands as generic.
A biography fact with an unrelated pitch reads worse than no personalisation.
Offering a demo, a trial, and a call at once means no decision gets made.
Walls of text do not get read cold.
Disruptive, innovative, synergy, leverage, cutting-edge, game-changing all mark the email as marketing copy.
A strong machine-written tell; rewrite the sentence instead.

antiPatterns.pattern: Fake RE:/FWD: thread prefixes on a first touch
antiPatterns.why: A deceptive subject line: a compliance violation and a trust killer even when it lifts opens.
Replacing a banned word with a synonym keeps the same weak idea; rewrite the idea underneath the line instead.
A researched opener bolted onto process-first body copy still loses; personalization supports the message, it cannot substitute for it.
Renting verified third-party profiles for outreach is identity deception and a platform-terms violation; scale with owned domains and inboxes instead.

benchmarks.fix: wrong personas or too much volume

seniorityVoice.lead: business outcome; one question, no options
the specific problem their team faces; one proof point
a day-to-day pain or a tool they recognise; technical detail acceptable
